title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 13
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A transport authority installed shelters at bus stops and reports that passenger numbers on the affected routes rose. It concludes that shelters attract passengers.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Shelters were installed during the summer.
B. Some shelters were vandalised.
C. Passengers report that the shelters are comfortable.
D. The authority installed shelters at the stops where passenger numbers had been growing fastest, in order to serve the most people.
E. The routes affected serve the city centre.
questions.explanation: The selection rule means growth preceded the shelters, so the rise cannot be attributed to them. A offers a rival cause but a weaker one, since it would affect all routes.

questions.prompt: A bottled water company argues that its product is more environmentally responsible than a competitor's because its bottles contain 30 per cent less plastic.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the argument?
options: A. How much the two products cost
B. Whether the lighter bottles are transported and disposed of in ways that make their total impact lower
C. Whether consumers can taste a difference
D. How long the company has been in business
E. Whether the competitor advertises nationally
questions.explanation: A comparison on one input does not establish a comparison overall; transport, recycling rates and end-of-life handling can reverse it.

questions.prompt: A cinema chain lowered ticket prices on Tuesdays and reports that Tuesday attendance has doubled. It concludes that lower prices increase cinema attendance.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Tuesday was previously the quietest day of the week.
B. The chain also refurbished several screens.
C. Some customers buy tickets online.
D. Concession sales rose on Tuesdays.
E. Attendance on other days fell by an amount close to the Tuesday increase.
questions.explanation: Shifting the same audience between days is not an increase in attendance; the total is unchanged. C is a rival cause but does not address the displacement.

questions.prompt: A supermarket introduced labels indicating higher welfare standards for chicken and reports that sales of labelled chicken rose sharply. It concludes that customers are willing to pay more for higher welfare.
questions.question: The conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. The labelled chicken was priced higher than the unlabelled chicken it replaced.
B. Welfare standards are independently verified.
C. Customers read the labels carefully.
D. The supermarket advertised the change.
E. Unlabelled chicken remained available.
questions.explanation: If the labelled product was not dearer, rising sales show a preference but say nothing about willingness to pay more. B and C bear on whether the label is meaningful rather than on the price inference.

questions.prompt: Every research grant awarded by the Halvorsen Trust last year went to a project with a named industrial partner. No project with an industrial partner published its results without a delay for commercial review. Some projects funded by the Trust published without delay.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Industrial partners cause publication delays.
B. Most Trust projects have industrial partners.
C. Some projects that published without delay were not funded last year.
D. No Trust project publishes promptly.
E. Projects without partners receive less money.
questions.explanation: Publishing without delay implies no industrial partner, and every grant awarded last year had one, so those projects were funded in some other year. B asserts causation the statements do not establish.

questions.prompt: A city introduced a toll on its river bridge and reports that traffic across the bridge has fallen by a quarter, presenting this as a reduction in congestion.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the city's presentation?
options: A. The toll is collected electronically.
B. Some drivers now travel at different times of day.
C. The toll raised more revenue than forecast.
D. Traffic on the untolled bridge two miles upstream has risen by nearly the same volume, and journey times there have worsened.
E. Cyclists are exempt from the toll.
questions.explanation: Diverted traffic relocates congestion rather than reducing it, so the city's measure captures only one side of the effect. C is a genuine response but consistent with an overall improvement.

questions.prompt: A school banned mobile telephones and reports that examination results improved the following year. The head teacher attributes the improvement to the ban.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the attribution?
options: A. Pupils say they concentrate better without their telephones.
B. The school also appointed a new head of mathematics.
C. In a group of comparable schools that adopted the ban in staggered years, results improved in each school in the year the ban took effect and not before.
D. Results improved nationally that year.
E. Parents supported the ban.
questions.explanation: Staggered adoption is the strongest observational design available here: the effect follows the treatment in time across several schools. C and D supply rival explanations.

questions.prompt: A warehouse requires all forklift operators to complete a training course. It reports that operators who scored highest on the course assessment have the fewest accidents, and proposes to promote high scorers to supervisory roles.
questions.question: The proposal is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes that assessment scores measure the qualities a supervisor needs, rather than only those a safe operator needs
B. ignores the cost of running the course
C. does not consider operators' length of service
D. relies on accident records compiled internally
E. overlooks the possibility that some accidents go unreported
questions.explanation: The evidence supports a claim about operating safely; supervision requires different capacities, so the inference crosses from one role to another without support.

questions.prompt: A hospital outsourced its cleaning and reports that cleaning costs fell by 30 per cent, describing the change as a saving.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the hospital's description?
options: A. The contractor employs fewer staff than the hospital did.
B. Some cleaning staff transferred to the contractor.
C. The contract runs for five years.
D. Other hospitals have outsourced cleaning.
E. Rates of hospital-acquired infection rose after the change, and the cost of treating them exceeds the amount saved.
questions.explanation: A cost that moves to another budget is not a saving; the comparison must be of total cost, not of the line item that fell.

questions.prompt: A museum found that visitors who enter through its shop spend more per head than those who enter through the main door, and plans to route all visitors through the shop.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. The shop is smaller than the main entrance hall.
B. The shop entrance is used mainly by visitors arriving by car, who are on average wealthier and stay longer than those arriving on foot.
C. The shop sells books and postcards.
D. Some visitors leave through the shop as well.
E. The museum charges no admission fee.
questions.explanation: The spending difference tracks who uses each entrance, not the entrance itself, so redirecting everyone need not change what anyone spends.

questions.prompt: The developer of a weather application argues that its forecasts are more accurate than a rival's, citing that its users report satisfaction more often.
questions.question: The argument is most vulnerable to the objection that it
options: A. does not specify the period over which forecasts were compared
B. ignores the rival's larger user base
C. assumes users check the forecast daily
D. treats user satisfaction as a measure of forecast accuracy
E. relies on a self-selected sample of respondents
questions.explanation: Satisfaction tracks interface, notifications and expectation as much as accuracy, and accuracy is directly measurable against outcomes — so the argument substitutes a proxy where the real quantity is available.

questions.passageText:
Economists have long divided advertising into two kinds. Informative advertising tells buyers that a product exists, what it costs and where to find it; persuasive advertising changes what buyers want without telling them anything. The distinction is analytically convenient and, applied to actual advertisements, almost impossible to sustain.

Consider an advertisement consisting of a brand name and an image. It appears to convey no information, and on the informative account it should be worthless. Yet a firm that spends heavily on such advertising is demonstrating something a buyer can use: that it expects repeat purchases sufficient to recover the outlay, which a firm selling a product nobody buys twice cannot afford to do. The expenditure is informative precisely because it is conspicuous and unrecoverable, and its content is irrelevant to that function.

A third account treats advertising as complementary to the product. On this view an advertisement does not deceive the buyer into valuing a watch more highly; it changes what owning the watch is, because part of what the owner obtains is that others have seen the advertisement too. Whether this is manipulation or the creation of genuine value is not a question economics can settle, and the honest treatments say so.

The policy consequence is that the standard regulatory instrument — requiring claims to be truthful — reaches only the smallest part of what advertising does. Most spending makes no factual claim at all, and the effects that concern critics operate through channels that truthfulness rules were never designed to touch.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that heavy spending on an advertisement conveying no factual content can still inform buyers because it
options: A. establishes the firm's legal responsibility for its claims
B. makes the product easier to find in shops
C. reduces the price the firm can charge
D. signals that the product is new to the market
E. demonstrates that the firm expects repeat purchases sufficient to recover the outlay
questions.explanation: The signalling argument: the expenditure is conspicuous and unrecoverable, which is what makes it credible, and its content is irrelevant to that function.

questions.passageText:
Detecting life on a planet orbiting another star means detecting it in the light of that planet's atmosphere. Certain gases are proposed as biosignatures, on the reasoning that they are produced in quantity by living processes and destroyed rapidly enough that a persistent supply implies continuous production.

Oxygen is the standard example, and its history illustrates the difficulty. For decades, abundant atmospheric oxygen was treated as near-proof of life, until modelling showed several ways a planet could accumulate oxygen without biology — photochemical splitting of water followed by loss of hydrogen to space being the best studied. The response was not to abandon oxygen but to require context: oxygen together with a reducing gas such as methane is harder to explain abiotically, since the two react and their simultaneous presence implies replenishment of both.

That is the general shape of the field's progress. Single-gas criteria have repeatedly failed, and the surviving proposals are about disequilibrium — combinations of substances that should not coexist unless something maintains them. Even these can be challenged, because the space of possible abiotic chemistry is not fully mapped and absence of a known mechanism is not absence of one.

The practical difficulty is that the detections available in the near term will be marginal: a few molecules, at low significance, on planets whose surface conditions are inferred rather than observed. In that regime the discipline that matters is not instrumental but interpretive, and the field's most useful recent work has been on how a claim of detection should be graded rather than on what to look for.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the reasoning behind proposing a gas as a biosignature is that it is
options: A. found only on planets with liquid water
B. produced in quantity by life and destroyed fast enough that persistence implies continuous production
C. easy to detect at low concentrations
D. absent from the atmospheres of gas giants
E. chemically inert
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph. E is close to the opposite of the requirement.

questions.passageText:
Few propositions attract as much agreement among economists as the claim that rent control reduces the supply and quality of rental housing, and few are as poorly served by the way that agreement is usually reported.

The mechanism is not in dispute. A price ceiling below the market rate reduces the return to supplying rental housing, so less of it is supplied: owners convert units to other uses, defer maintenance, or sell to owner-occupiers. Studies of cities that imposed strict controls have found substantial reductions in the rental stock, and the tenants who benefit are those already housed, while those seeking housing face a smaller supply.

What the summary omits is that the policies actually being enacted are frequently not the ones the classic analysis addresses. Second-generation controls limit the rate of increase within a tenancy rather than setting an absolute ceiling, exempt new construction, and permit increases between tenancies. Their effects are smaller and more mixed, and treating evidence about strict ceilings as though it settled the case against these measures conflates different instruments.

The stronger argument is a different one. Controls of any kind address a symptom of a supply constraint without touching the constraint, and where the binding limit is the number of dwellings a city permits to be built, distributing scarce units differently cannot produce more of them. That argument holds against second-generation controls too, and it is the one worth making — but it is an argument for building, not merely an argument against tenants' protections.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that under a strict price ceiling, the tenants who benefit are
options: A. those seeking housing for the first time
B. owner-occupiers
C. landlords with large portfolios
D. tenants in newly constructed buildings
E. those already housed
questions.explanation: Those seeking housing face a smaller supply, which is the distributional point the passage draws.

questions.passageText:
Oral history and legal testimony both rest on memory, and research over the past half century has shown memory to be reconstructive rather than reproductive. Each recollection is assembled from fragments, and the assembly is influenced by what has been learned, said and asked since.

The practical findings are consistent. Confidence and accuracy are only loosely related, so a witness's certainty is a poor guide to reliability. The wording of a question shapes what is recalled, and repeated questioning can install details that were never present. Memory for the gist of an event is considerably more durable than memory for particulars, which is inconvenient, because particulars are what cross-examination and archival research both pursue.

The wrong inference from this is that testimony is worthless. Central details of significant events are recalled with reasonable accuracy over long periods, and the errors that occur are patterned rather than random: they cluster in peripheral detail, in the sequence of events, and in the attribution of a memory to its source. Knowing where errors concentrate is more useful than a general suspicion.

For oral history the implication is procedural rather than sceptical. An interview should be recorded rather than summarised, questions should be open rather than leading, and the interviewer's own contribution should be preserved in the record so that later users can see what was asked. What is being collected is not a transcript of the past but a person's account of it, and an account whose conditions of production are documented is a better historical source than one presented as unmediated recall.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that a witness's confidence is
options: A. a reliable guide to accuracy
B. impossible to assess
C. higher for peripheral than for central details
D. only loosely related to accuracy
E. unaffected by repeated questioning
questions.explanation: Stated among the practical findings; the passage also notes repeated questioning can install details, which tells against E.

Oral history and legal testimony both rest on memory, and research over the past half century has shown memory to be reconstructive rather than reproductive. Each recollection is assembled from fragments, and the assembly is influenced by what has been learned, said and asked since.

The practical findings are consistent. Confidence and accuracy are only loosely related, so a witness's certainty is a poor guide to reliability. The wording of a question shapes what is recalled, and repeated questioning can install details that were never present. Memory for the gist of an event is considerably more durable than memory for particulars, which is inconvenient, because particulars are what cross-examination and archival research both pursue.

The wrong inference from this is that testimony is worthless. Central details of significant events are recalled with reasonable accuracy over long periods, and the errors that occur are patterned rather than random: they cluster in peripheral detail, in the sequence of events, and in the attribution of a memory to its source. Knowing where errors concentrate is more useful than a general suspicion.

For oral history the implication is procedural rather than sceptical. An interview should be recorded rather than summarised, questions should be open rather than leading, and the interviewer's own contribution should be preserved in the record so that later users can see what was asked. What is being collected is not a transcript of the past but a person's account of it, and an account whose conditions of production are documented is a better historical source than one presented as unmediated recall.
